newsitem.title: USA: Freemen disciples convicted in check-cashing scam.
newsitem.headline: Freemen disciples convicted in check-cashing scam.

text.p: Three followers of the Freemen anti-government group were convicted Friday of fraud and money laundering in a multimillion-dollar check-cashing scam, prosecutors said.

A federal jury found Elizabeth Broderick guilty of 26 felony counts in connection with the distribution of fraudulent checks purportedly payable by the U.S. government, U.S. Attorney Nora Manella said.
Two co-conspirators were convicted of fewer felony counts -- Julian Cheney of 16 and Barry Switzer of 11.

Prosecutors depicted the three as disciples of the Freemen, an extremist group that surrendered to FBI agents June 13 after an 81-day armed standoff at a remote Montana ranch. Sixteen members of the Freemen were taken into custody near Jordan, Montana.
Broderick, who called herself the "Lien Queen," was trained last year at a Freemen seminar in Jordan on how to issue the fraudulent checks, prosecutors said.

In keeping with militant Freemen beliefs, Broderick, who has a past conviction for running a pyramid scheme in Colorado, denied being subject to U.S. laws or the sovereignty of state and federal governments.
"Behind Ms. Broderick's anti-government rhetoric was a classic con artist," Manella said in a statement. "She appealed principally to financially strapped people who wanted something for nothing."

Prosecutors said Broderick distributed the checks at workshops she held in southern California on how to pay off debt. She charged up to $200 per student for the classes plus a fee for the checks, which she called "comptroller warrants" that she said could be used to avoid payment of debt.

The scam involved the sale of about 8,000 phony checks for amounts totalling millions of dollars, prosecutors said. They said Broderick and her conspirators netted more than $1 million from the warrants.
Broderick, Switzer and Cheney are scheduled to be sentenced Jan. 6.
In August Broderick's business partner, Adolf Karl Hoch, pleaded guilty to 15 felony charges stemming from the fraudulent check scheme. He is scheduled to be sentenced in November.
